headline: Growth ran hot at 3.4% and inflation stayed sticky, but an AI-earnings rout sent money into bonds and pulled the 10-year back below 5%.
dateline: Friday, October 30, 2026 · closes as of Thu Oct 29

rundown.h: Alphabet lost about $482 billion in one session.
rundown.p: Alphabet's record one-day drop erased roughly $482 billion of market value Thursday, per Yahoo Finance, the second-largest single-day loss for a U.S. stock after Nvidia's in January 2025. Analysts pointed to capital spending running near 40% of quarterly revenue and doubts over when AI outlays pay off. It remains the fourth-largest company, worth more than $3.4 trillion.

rundown.h: Amazon's cloud sped up, but the cash went out faster.
rundown.p: Amazon's third-quarter sales rose 12% to $201.9 billion and AWS grew 39% to $46.0 billion, its fastest pace in nearly five years. It kept its roughly $220 billion 2026 capital spending plan, and trailing free cash flow swung to an outflow of $42.4 billion from a $14.8 billion inflow. Shares fell about 6% after hours, after closing down 4.25%.

rundown.h: Caterpillar beat estimates and still had its worst day since 2020.
rundown.p: Caterpillar slid 9.3% Thursday, per Bloomberg, its steepest one-day drop since March 2020, even after adjusted earnings of $7.20 a share on $20.68 billion of revenue topped forecasts. Investors fixated on a call for only modest fourth-quarter growth despite a record backlog. The stock, a big winner of the AI power buildout, is down nearly 40% from its June peak.

rundown.h: Intel's outlook sank the stock after hours.
rundown.p: Intel guided fourth-quarter revenue to $15 billion to $16 billion, below the $17.07 billion expected, with adjusted earnings of 25 cents against 43 cents. It cited a PC slump it expects to last into the first half of 2027, higher memory costs and an incident at its Israel plant worth about $600 million in lost revenue. Shares fell roughly 16% to 23% after hours.

rundown.h: Big Oil is cashing in; Exxon and Chevron report today.
rundown.p: BP's third-quarter underlying profit hit $8.5 billion, up from $2.2 billion a year earlier and well above the $6.19 billion expected, as its refining margin jumped to $46.70 a barrel from $29.60 in the second quarter. Exxon Mobil and Chevron report this morning. The World Bank's new forecast has Brent averaging $92 this year, about $23 below Thursday's settle.
rundown.src: Reuters via The Private Banker · Oct 30

rundown.h: ADT agreed to go private at a 46% premium.
rundown.p: Home-security company ADT agreed to be bought by Thrive Holdings for $10 a share in cash, about $7.6 billion of equity value and $15.3 billion including debt, a 45.6% premium to its Oct 27 close. The deal is expected to close in the first quarter of 2027, pending shareholder and antitrust approval, and would take ADT private.

dive.title: Your building is getting cheaper to insure. Your tenant's trucks are not.
dive.dek: Commercial insurance prices are splitting in two: property rates are falling by double digits while liability keeps climbing.
dive.body:
For once, an insurance story that isn't all bad news. Marsh's Global Insurance Market Index, out Oct. 21, shows global commercial rates fell 5% in the third quarter, the ninth quarterly decline in a row. The U.S. composite slipped just 1%, and that small number hides a big split: U.S. property rates fell 10% (after 13% in the second quarter), while U.S. casualty rose 6% and risk-adjusted umbrella and excess cover jumped 13%.

Why the split? On the property side, insurers have plenty of capacity, competition is stiff and the U.S. hurricane season has been mild; big catastrophe-exposed programs fell 13%. Liability is a different story. Chubb's CEO says loss costs are still running well ahead of general inflation, and Marsh notes auto loss ratios have topped 100% for more than a decade. Size matters too. Ivans' small-commercial renewal data (Oct. 28) still shows property up 5.65%, umbrella up 6.88% and commercial auto up 3.63%. At Chubb, big shared-and-layered property accounts fell 11% while small and mid-size property rose slightly. The discount goes to the big buyers.

Why it matters: Owners with sizable, institutional property programs get a modest NOI tailwind just as a 10-year near 5% squeezes valuations. Industrial and IOS landlords should look at both sides of the lease, though. Their tenants are fleets, contractors and equipment yards, and those businesses pay for auto and umbrella cover, the lines still rising. Higher liability bills eat into tenant margins and make lease-required coverage limits pricier to carry.

What would change it: Soft markets end when losses show up. Hurricane season runs through Nov. 30, and the Jan. 1 reinsurance renewals set the tone for 2027. Insurers are still making money (Kinsale posted a 75.4% combined ratio) but are easing off on rate: W.R. Berkley's increases halved to 4%. Then there's the war. Hormuz war-risk cover went from 0.15–0.25% of hull value before the conflict to 3–10% at its peak earlier this year, a reminder that a shock can spread through marine and energy lines fast.

items.title: Q3 GDP grew at a 3.4% annualized pace, the fastest in a year, on equipment spending and inventories

chart.t: Real GDP, % change at an annualized rate
chart.src: Source: BEA via FRED (A191RL1Q225SBEA), updated Oct 29, 2026.

items.body:
The economy grew at a 3.4% annualized rate in the third quarter, released Thursday, above the 3.2% consensus and up from 2.2% in the second quarter; it was the fastest pace in a year. Consumer spending rose 3.8%, matching Q2 and adding 2.52 points. Private investment added 3.27 points, with equipment up 20.9%, which Trading Economics ties largely to AI. Inventories added 1.61 points and government spending rose 5.3%, helped by Strategic Petroleum Reserve crude sales. Imports jumped 19.7%, subtracting 2.64 points, and residential investment fell 3.3%.

September PCE prices, out the same morning, rose 0.5% on the month and 3.6% from a year earlier, both in line; energy rose 9.2% in the month. Core PCE rose 0.3% and 3.1%, also in line. Real consumer spending was flat and the saving rate slipped to 3.8%.

Treasury yields fell anyway, with the 2-year down 6 basis points to 4.61% and the 10-year down 7 to 4.98%, as a tech-led stock selloff drove buyers into bonds. CME FedWatch odds of a December hike eased to about 75–78% from 84%.

experts.who: Chris Osmond, CIO, Fifth Third Wealth Advisors
experts.view: The economy is outrunning expectations while still producing more inflation than the Fed is comfortable with, which could push yields and the FOMC in a hawkish direction.

experts.who: Andrew Husby, senior U.S. economist, BNP Paribas
experts.view: Underneath the headline the economy is performing well, with the AI buildout a support but not the only engine of growth.

experts.who: Kevin Warsh, Fed Chair (Oct 28, before the data)
experts.view: Most of his colleagues don't judge the economy to be running hot.

items.lean: Osmond reads the report as pressure toward a December hike; Husby sees solid underlying growth; Warsh said this week most Fed colleagues don't see overheating.
items.src: Sources: BEA via Trading Economics (GDP, core PCE, personal spending pages, Oct 29–30); Investing.com; Yahoo Finance/CFO Dive; FRED; Closing Look (yields, FedWatch).

lead.title: Talks stall, the Houthis widen the fight, and the Pentagon briefs on options
lead.body:
The diplomacy track is alive but not moving. A senior Iranian official dismissed a new Qatari-mediated draft as unacceptable and not a real offer, while Iran's foreign minister said Tehran is still giving diplomacy a chance. The Wall Street Journal reported that the U.S. military's top Middle East commander briefed President Trump on military options Thursday, keeping alive fears of strikes after the Nov 3 midterms.

The fighting spread along the Gulf's oil infrastructure. The Houthis claimed attacks on Saudi Arabia's Ras Tanura and Rabigh refineries and an Aramco facility at Abqaiq, which Riyadh hasn't confirmed; the Saudi-led coalition said it destroyed a ballistic missile aimed at the Eastern Province early Thursday. Iran's Revolutionary Guards said three tankers hit mines and caught fire on an unauthorized route south of Hormuz in 24 hours. ExxonMobil and Chevron pulled executives from next week's big UAE oil show over security.
lead.reach: Through oil. Brent settled down 0.38% at $114.88 on Oct 29 after falling more than $2 intraday, then traded near $116 Friday morning; it is up nearly 14% in October, on track for a fourth monthly gain.

views.view: Renewed efforts to de-escalate with Iran are what's been pressing on prices.
Reports of fresh Houthi attacks pulled oil off its lows, and mixed Russian signals on diesel supply are helping hold prices up.

reading.title: Defense wins championships (and portfolios)
reading.dek: Paul Tudor Jones built a legendary macro career on one unglamorous idea: worry about losses first, and let the gains take care of themselves.
reading.body:
Halloween is tomorrow, but the scariest stuff is already on your screen: a 10-year yield hovering near 5%, oil above $100 as the Iran war squeezes supply, and a Fed that sounds more eager to hike than cut. That makes it a fine week to borrow the playbook of Paul Tudor Jones, the macro trader who starts with a question most investors skip. Not how much can I make, but how do I avoid getting wiped out.

First, a quick refresher. Jones was born in Memphis in 1954, earned an economics degree from the University of Virginia in 1976 and learned cotton futures in New Orleans under broker Eli Tullis. Tullis later fired him for falling asleep at his desk after a night out, which makes for a humbling origin story. After a stint as a commodities broker at E.F. Hutton, he founded Tudor Investment Corporation in 1980. His big moment came in 1987, when the fund reportedly returned about 126% after fees, largely on short bets.

His framework comes down to defense first, and it rests on three ideas. One: he knows what he's willing to lose before he enters a trade, so the exit is built into the plan from day one. Two: he hunts for lopsided payoffs. He has described looking for trades that risk $1 to make $5. At those odds you can be wrong four times out of five and still come out ahead, so being right matters less than how much each mistake costs. Three: he uses a trend filter. He told Tony Robbins that anything sliding below its 200-day moving average is a reason to get out. It's simple and almost boring, and that's the point, because a mechanical rule keeps your ego out of the decision.

The logic is just arithmetic. A 50% loss needs a 100% gain to get back to even, so avoiding the big hole matters more than catching every rally. According to Jones, the 200-day rule had him flat at the top of the 1987 crash. It isn't a crystal ball, though. Trend rules get whipsawed in choppy markets, and sometimes you'll sell right before a bounce. Still, a small, known cost beats a ruinous one.

Why it matters now: when rates climb, being wrong gets more expensive. Long-duration assets take the biggest hit when discount rates rise, and oil can reverse on a single ceasefire headline. Playing defense doesn't mean sitting in cash. It means you pick your exit before the market picks it for you.

quote.text: At the very top of the crash, I was flat.
quote.src: Paul Tudor Jones, interview with Tony Robbins (MONEY: Master the Game)

takeaways: 10Y near 5%: higher rates raise the cost of being wrong. Size positions accordingly.
Oil above $100 can reverse on one ceasefire headline. Set exits before entering.
Fed leaning toward hikes? Check which holdings sit below their 200-day averages.
